explanation: Checking in with her privately later gives her space to share as much or as little as she wants without putting her on the spot, which is what showing empathy looks like right after a loss. Assigning her the lightest tasks without asking decides what she needs instead of finding out, asking her to explain her short answers in front of the group exposes her in a moment she is clearly struggling with, and ignoring the short answers entirely dismisses what she is visibly going through.

question: A team member's presentation to a major client falls apart when the client abruptly cancels the meeting five minutes in over an unrelated contract dispute, and the team member is visibly shaken afterward, having spent three weeks preparing. Which response best shows empathy?

options.A: Move straight into planning the rescheduled meeting
options.B: Acknowledge how frustrating that must feel
options.C: Point out that the cancellation was not about his work
options.D: Tell him the three weeks were not wasted since the client will reschedule

explanation: Acknowledging how frustrating that must feel names what he is actually experiencing before moving on to anything else, which is what showing empathy requires in the moment right after the setback. Moving straight into planning the rescheduled meeting skips his feelings entirely in favor of the next task. Pointing out that the cancellation was not about his work tries to reassure him with logic before acknowledging how he feels. And telling him the three weeks were not wasted offers comfort about the outcome without first recognizing what he is feeling right now.

question: A marketing manager already has her team fully booked for the next two weeks when a director asks her to also take on an urgent rebrand project with no adjustment to the current deadlines. Which response best demonstrates assertiveness?

options.A: State that the team cannot absorb it without a trade-off
options.B: Agree immediately without raising any concerns
options.C: Tell the director the request is unreasonable and walk away
options.D: Accept the project as asked and quietly reassign the current deadlines later

explanation: Stating plainly that the team cannot absorb the new project without a trade-off on an existing deadline raises the real constraint directly to the person who can act on it, which is what assertiveness looks like when a request exceeds current capacity. Agreeing immediately without raising any concerns is passive and sets the team up to miss a deadline it never had the chance to renegotiate. Telling the director the request is completely unreasonable and walking away is aggressive rather than assertive, since it shuts down the conversation instead of proposing a solution. And accepting the project while quietly reassigning deadlines later avoids the direct conversation altogether and leaves the director unaware of the real trade-off being made.

performanceIndicator: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
question: Vantage Outdoor Gear meets every literal requirement of a state's product-warning law by printing the mandated safety text on its packaging, but sets the type at a size most shoppers cannot read without a magnifying glass. Which best characterizes Vantage's compliance?

options.A: A violation of the warning statute itself
options.B: Full compliance, letter and intent alike
options.C: Legal in form, not in spirit
options.D: An unrelated unfair-competition claim about pricing

explanation: Vantage satisfies the literal text of the warning statute but defeats its purpose by making the required disclosure unreadable, which is compliance in form rather than in spirit. The other options either wrongly claim the statute's literal text is violated, claim full compliance without qualification, or recast the issue as an unrelated unfair-competition claim that has nothing to do with the warning statute.

performanceIndicator: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
question: SteelForge Manufacturing schedules every safety inspection required by law and never misses one, but always tells the affected production line the exact date and time in advance so hazards can be hidden until the inspector leaves. How should this practice be characterized?

options.A: Satisfies the letter, defeats the intent
options.B: A missed inspection requirement
options.C: A courtesy notice most regulators require in practice
options.D: Full regulatory compliance

explanation: SteelForge meets every literal inspection requirement but times its notice so hazards are hidden precisely when the inspector is present, defeating the safety law's purpose even though no inspection is missed. The other options either wrongly claim an inspection was skipped, mistake an informal notice practice for full compliance with the law's intent, or ignore the concealment altogether.

performanceIndicator: Comply with the spirit and intent of laws and regulations
question: Driftwood Diner schedules the one daily walk-in-cooler temperature log required by the health code, but always records it at the single hour each day when the cooler happens to run coldest, ignoring how the cooler performs the rest of the day. How should this practice be characterized?

options.A: A pattern several health inspectors have accepted without objection in the past
options.B: Meets the minimum logging rule while hiding the cooler's true daily swings
options.C: A missed daily temperature-logging requirement entirely
options.D: Full compliance with the law's letter and its purpose

explanation: Driftwood logs a temperature once each day exactly as the health code requires, so no logging requirement is missed. But choosing the single coldest hour to record hides the cooler's actual conditions for the rest of the day, which defeats the law's purpose of catching real risk. That is compliance with the letter of the rule while undermining its intent, not full compliance and not a missed log.

question: Meridian Fabrication wants to add a second shift and run heavy equipment through the night at its current site, located in an area zoned for light industrial use only. What legal issue does this raise?

options.A: A workplace-safety violation
options.B: An unrelated tax-filing compliance issue
options.C: A zoning-compliance issue over permitted land use
options.D: A breach of its supplier contract terms

explanation: Meridian's plan to run heavy equipment at night in an area zoned for light industrial use raises a zoning-compliance question about whether that use and those hours are permitted at the site. The other options describe unrelated business problems that the facts never raise.

question: Coastal Textiles installs a new dyeing line that discharges treated wastewater into the municipal sewer at a volume well above what its existing industrial discharge permit authorizes, even though the water tests within safety limits. What legal issue does this raise?

options.A: A water-safety violation despite testing within safe limits
options.B: A straightforward increase in normal operating costs only
options.C: A permit-compliance issue because the discharge volume exceeds its authorized limit
options.D: A minor, routine administrative filing delay only

explanation: Coastal Textiles is discharging more wastewater than its industrial discharge permit allows, which is a permit-compliance problem regardless of whether the water itself tests safe. Meeting a safety threshold does not substitute for staying within an authorized volume, so this is not a water-safety violation on these facts. It is also more than a routine cost increase or a paperwork delay, since operating outside the permit's terms is itself the legal issue.

performanceIndicator: Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
question: Bramblewood Kitchenware designs a distinctive spoon-shaped logo it wants only its brand to use in commerce. Which method protects it?

options.A: A utility patent application
options.B: A copyright filing that covers only the logo's artwork
options.C: Federal trademark registration
options.D: A confidentiality agreement with employees

explanation: A logo used to identify Bramblewood's brand in commerce is protected through federal trademark registration, not a patent or copyright, since it functions as a source identifier rather than a useful invention or a work whose artistic expression alone is being protected. The other options each protect a different kind of intellectual property that does not fit a brand-identifying logo.

performanceIndicator: Describe methods used to protect intellectual property
question: Solstice Beverage Co. keeps its syrup recipe known to only two employees, stores it in a locked safe, and never files any public application describing it. Which method is it using to protect the recipe?

options.A: A utility patent publicly disclosing the recipe formula
options.B: A copyright registered for the recipe's formula
options.C: A trademark filed for the brand name on the bottle
options.D: Trade-secret protection through strict confidentiality

explanation: Keeping the recipe limited to two employees and locked away, with no public filing, is how a business protects a trade secret -- secrecy itself is the protection, and it lasts only as long as the confidentiality does. Filing for a patent would require publicly disclosing the exact formula, which defeats the purpose here, and neither a copyright nor a trademark protects a functional recipe.

performanceIndicator: Describe the United States' judicial system
question: A small business in Ohio wants to sue a supplier, also based in Ohio, over a $40,000 contract dispute involving only state contract law. Which court would normally hear the case first?

options.A: A state trial court in Ohio
options.B: A federal district court under its diversity jurisdiction
options.C: A state appellate court on direct review
options.D: The U.S. Supreme Court

explanation: Because both the business and the supplier are Ohio residents and the claim rests on state contract law, the case begins in an Ohio state trial court, not federal court -- diversity jurisdiction requires parties from different states. A state appellate court only hears the case after a trial-court decision is appealed, and the U.S. Supreme Court hears only a small fraction of cases, virtually never as a first stop.

performanceIndicator: Describe the United States' judicial system
question: A California business believes a competitor, also based in California, is infringing its federally registered trademark in violation of the federal Lanham Act. Even though both parties are from the same state, which court can properly hear the case?

options.A: A state trial court, since both parties share the same state
options.B: A state appellate court, bypassing the trial level
options.C: The U.S. Supreme Court, taken as the first forum
options.D: A federal district court, since the claim arises under a federal law

explanation: Because the claim arises under the federal Lanham Act, it presents a federal question, and federal district courts have jurisdiction over federal-question claims regardless of where the parties are located -- same-state parties only rules out diversity jurisdiction, not federal-question jurisdiction. A state trial court is the wrong forum for a federal statutory claim, an appellate court cannot hear a case with no trial-court record yet, and the Supreme Court is not a first-instance forum for ordinary infringement suits.

performanceIndicator: Describe the nature of customs regulations
question: Lakeview Furnishings imports a container of finished wood chairs from overseas. Before the goods can be released for sale in the U.S., what must it do?

options.A: Hire a customs broker first
options.B: Classify the goods and pay the applicable duty
options.C: Obtain a new import license each time
options.D: Wait for a customs audit

explanation: Before imported goods can be released for sale, the importer must classify them under the correct tariff schedule and pay any duty that classification requires -- that is the core customs-compliance step. A customs broker can help but is not legally required for every shipment, a new import license is not needed for routine commercial goods, and there is no requirement to wait for an audit before selling.

performanceIndicator: Describe the nature of customs regulations
question: A customs officer discovers that Solene Apparel understated the declared value of an imported shipment on its entry paperwork. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: No consequence at all here
options.B: An immediate criminal referral over the misdeclared value
options.C: A temporary suspension of its import license
options.D: Penalties plus a reassessment of duty owed

explanation: Understating a shipment's declared value to reduce duty is a customs violation, and the typical first consequence is penalties plus a reassessment of the duty actually owed, not an outcome as severe as an immediate criminal referral or a license suspension, and certainly not no consequence at all.

performanceIndicator: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
question: Two neighbors shake hands on a deal for one to sell the other a parcel of land for $60,000, with nothing put in writing. What is the legal status of this agreement?

options.A: Unenforceable, since land sales need a signed writing
options.B: Fully binding once spoken aloud
options.C: Voidable at either neighbor's discretion
options.D: Void from the moment it was made

explanation: Contracts for the sale of land generally must be in writing to be enforceable under the Statute of Frauds, so a handshake deal for real estate is unenforceable even though both parties agreed. It is not automatically binding just because it was spoken, and 'voidable' and 'void' describe different legal defects that do not apply to a simple missing-writing problem.

performanceIndicator: Describe the nature of legally binding contracts
question: A wealthy uncle tells his niece in writing, 'I promise to give you $5,000 for your birthday next month,' but she gives nothing in return. Can she legally enforce this promise?

options.A: Yes, since it is written down
options.B: No, since a notarized signature is required
options.C: Yes, since family gift promises are widely honored
options.D: No, since it lacks consideration

explanation: A promise to make a gift is not legally enforceable without consideration -- something of value given in return -- and the niece gave nothing, so she cannot enforce it even though the promise is in writing. Being written down does not supply consideration, family custom does not create a legal obligation, and notarization is not what is missing here.

performanceIndicator: Discuss the nature of debtor-creditor relationships
question: Harborline Equipment Rentals lends a construction company $30,000 and files a UCC financing statement listing the company's excavator as collateral. If the company defaults, what is Harborline's position relative to other creditors?

options.A: An unsecured general creditor
options.B: A guarantor of the company's other debts
options.C: A cosigner on the original loan
options.D: A secured creditor with first claim on the excavator

explanation: By filing a UCC financing statement against the excavator, Harborline becomes a secured creditor with a priority claim to that specific collateral ahead of creditors who lent without collateral. It is not an unsecured creditor, a guarantor (who backs someone else's debt), or a cosigner (who shares liability on the loan itself).

performanceIndicator: Discuss the nature of debtor-creditor relationships
question: After winning a lawsuit against a client who never paid an invoice, Fenwick Design Studio obtains a court order allowing it to collect part of the client's wages directly from the client's employer. What is this legal tool called?

options.A: A voluntary repayment plan the client agreed to
options.B: A court-ordered wage garnishment
options.C: A property repossession order
options.D: An involuntary bankruptcy filing

explanation: A court order letting a judgment creditor collect directly from a debtor's wages through the employer is a wage garnishment. It is not a voluntary repayment plan (the client isn't agreeing to it), a repossession (there's no secured property being seized), or a bankruptcy filing (that is a proceeding the debtor, not the creditor, initiates).

performanceIndicator: Discuss the role of administrative law
question: The Federal Trade Commission writes a detailed rule specifying exactly what claims a supplement maker must be able to substantiate before advertising 'clinically proven' results. What role is the FTC performing here?

options.A: Issuing a binding regulation
options.B: Deciding a private contract dispute
options.C: Passing a new statute
options.D: Conducting a criminal trial against the maker

explanation: An agency writing a detailed rule that spells out what businesses must do to comply is exercising its rulemaking authority, one of administrative law's core functions. It is not deciding a specific dispute between two parties, passing a statute (that is Congress's role), or conducting a criminal trial.

performanceIndicator: Discuss the role of administrative law
question: A state licensing board holds a hearing, receives evidence, and revokes a contractor's license after finding repeated safety violations. What role is the board performing?

options.A: Administrative adjudication
options.B: Passing a new statute on contractor licensing
options.C: Conducting a criminal prosecution
options.D: Negotiating a private settlement

explanation: Holding a hearing, weighing evidence, and issuing a decision that revokes a specific license is administrative adjudication -- an agency acting in a court-like role over one case. It is not passing a statute (a legislative act), a criminal prosecution (a different proceeding with different rules), or a private negotiated settlement.

performanceIndicator: Discuss the role of administrative law
question: Before finalizing a new rule limiting the caffeine content advertisers can highlight in energy-drink marketing, the FTC publishes a draft rule, invites public comments for 60 days, and revises the rule based on the feedback it receives. Which administrative-law function best describes this process?

options.A: Informal guidance the agency may revise at will
options.B: An internal policy memo circulated without any public process
options.C: Notice-and-comment rulemaking, where the agency must weigh public input first
options.D: A judicial-style hearing limited to the parties directly regulated

explanation: Publishing a draft rule, taking public comments, and revising the rule in response is notice-and-comment rulemaking, the standard formal process agencies use to adopt binding regulations. It is not informal guidance the agency can change without process, an internal memo with no public input, and it is not a judicial-style hearing, since no specific regulated party is being individually judged -- the rule applies industry-wide.

performanceIndicator: Explain the nature of agency relationships
question: A purchasing clerk at Delmar Hardware orders industrial shelving from a new supplier without prior authorization. Delmar's owner later reviews the order, likes the terms, and tells the supplier the company will honor it. What has the owner done?

options.A: Terminated the clerk's agency relationship
options.B: Delegated new express authority
options.C: Created a new apparent-authority relationship going forward
options.D: Ratified the clerk's unauthorized act

explanation: By reviewing the unauthorized order after the fact and telling the supplier the company will honor it, the owner ratified the clerk's act, retroactively treating it as authorized. This is not a termination of the agency, a grant of new express authority for future orders, or the creation of apparent authority, which arises from how a principal represents an agent's authority in advance, not from approving something after it already happened.

performanceIndicator: Explain the nature of agency relationships
question: A talent agent represents a musician and also owns a stake in a concert venue. Without telling the musician, the agent books all of her shows at that venue. What duty has the agent most clearly breached?

options.A: The duty of obedience
options.B: The duty to keep accurate records of every booking
options.C: The duty of loyalty
options.D: The duty of reasonable care and skill

explanation: By secretly booking shows at a venue in which he has a financial stake, the agent puts his own interest ahead of the musician's, which is a breach of the duty of loyalty -- an agent must disclose and avoid self-dealing conflicts. This is not a failure to follow instructions, keep records, or exercise ordinary skill; the problem here is the undisclosed conflict of interest itself.

performanceIndicator: Explain the nature of import/export law
question: Voss Optics wants to ship a batch of precision lenses to a country currently under a U.S. embargo. What must Voss do before the shipment can legally leave the country?

options.A: Obtain an export license or confirm it is exempt
options.B: File a standard customs entry form
options.C: Post a customs surety bond
options.D: Pay a modestly higher tariff rate

explanation: Shipping goods to an embargoed destination generally requires an export license, or written confirmation that the shipment qualifies for an exemption, before it can legally leave the country -- the embargo itself is the controlling issue, not routine customs paperwork. A standard customs form, a surety bond, or a higher tariff does not address the embargo restriction at all.

performanceIndicator: Explain the nature of import/export law
question: A retailer imports garments manufactured overseas and repackages them for sale under its own store brand. What must the retailer include on the garments to comply with import law?

options.A: A duplicate customs form
options.B: The country where the garment was made
options.C: The store's return policy
options.D: The manufacturer's full corporate address and tax ID

explanation: Country-of-origin labeling law requires imported garments to disclose where they were actually made, even when resold under a different store brand -- repackaging does not remove that requirement. A duplicate customs form, the store's return policy, and the manufacturer's corporate address are not what country-of-origin labeling requires.

performanceIndicator: Explain the nature of import/export law
question: A domestic steel producer petitions the government, arguing that a foreign competitor is selling steel in the U.S. market at prices below what it charges in its own home market, harming domestic producers. If the government agrees, what remedy is typically imposed?

options.A: An anti-dumping duty added on top of the imported price
options.B: A total embargo blocking every future shipment of foreign steel into the country
options.C: A fine paid to the domestic producer
options.D: A quota capping how much foreign steel may enter

explanation: When a government finds that a foreign producer is selling below its home-market price in a way that harms domestic industry, the typical remedy is an anti-dumping duty added on top of the import price to offset the price difference, not a full embargo, a quota, or a fine paid directly to the domestic competitor. A duty targets the unfair pricing specifically while still allowing the trade to continue at a corrected price.

question: Two investors form a business where one manages daily operations and has unlimited personal liability, while the other contributes capital only and risks nothing beyond that investment. What form of ownership is this?

options.A: A general partnership sharing unlimited liability equally
options.B: A limited partnership
options.C: A C corporation structure
options.D: A single-member LLC

explanation: One partner managing the business with unlimited personal liability while the other only contributes capital and risks no more than that investment describes a limited partnership, which has at least one general partner and at least one limited partner. A general partnership gives every partner unlimited liability, and a C corporation and an LLC both generally shield all owners from personal liability, which does not match either partner's position here.

question: A freelance photographer starts operating under her own name, files no formation paperwork with the state, and reports all business income on her personal tax return. What form of ownership is this?

options.A: A corporation formed once she begins earning income
options.B: A sole proprietorship
options.C: A single-member limited liability company
options.D: A general partnership

explanation: Operating under her own name with no formation filing and reporting income on her personal return is the default, unincorporated form: a sole proprietorship. A corporation and an LLC both require a formal state filing to exist, which never happened here, and a partnership requires more than one owner.

performanceIndicator: Identify the basic torts relating to business enterprises
question: A sales rep from a rival firm learns that Beacon Supply has an exclusive distribution contract with a retailer, then persuades the retailer to break that contract and switch suppliers. What tort has the rep most likely committed?

options.A: Fraudulent misrepresentation of terms
options.B: Trespass onto the retailer's property
options.C: Conversion of the retailer's inventory without permission
options.D: Tortious contract interference

explanation: Knowingly persuading a party to break an existing exclusive contract is tortious interference with contract, since the rep intentionally induced the breach for competitive advantage. It is not fraud (no false statement was made to Beacon), trespass (no property was entered), or conversion (nothing was taken).

performanceIndicator: Identify the basic torts relating to business enterprises
question: A rival firm's sales manager tells several of Beacon Supply's largest customers, falsely and without any basis, that Beacon's products fail safety testing, causing two customers to cancel their orders. What tort has occurred?

options.A: Breach of an implied warranty
options.B: Negligent misrepresentation made without any intent to deceive
options.C: Invasion of privacy
options.D: Product disparagement (trade libel)

explanation: Making false statements about a competitor's product that cause customers to cancel orders is product disparagement, also called trade libel -- it targets the product's reputation rather than a person's. It is not a breach of warranty (no sale or promise between the parties), invasion of privacy (no private fact was exposed), and unlike negligent misrepresentation, the statements here were made knowingly false, not merely careless.

question: A startup with a $500 total budget wants to know if a new flavor will sell before its next production run in two weeks. Which research approach is most appropriate?

options.A: A national telephone survey
options.B: A multi-city focus group study spanning several months
options.C: A syndicated industry data purchase
options.D: A quick informal taste test

explanation: With only $500 and two weeks before production, a quick informal taste test is the only approach that fits the startup's time and budget constraints. A national telephone survey, a multi-city focus-group study, and a syndicated data purchase are all legitimate research methods, but each costs far more money and time than this decision allows.

question: A national retail chain is deciding whether to spend $8 million relocating its flagship distribution center, a decision that will shape logistics costs for the next fifteen years. Which research approach is most appropriate given the size and permanence of this decision?

options.A: A single employee's informal, unrecorded opinion from one short hallway conversation
options.B: A single online poll posted for 24 hours
options.C: A brief hallway survey of ten customers
options.D: A rigorous, multi-method study combining site data and cost modeling

explanation: An $8 million, fifteen-year decision this consequential calls for a rigorous, multi-method study combining site data and cost modeling, not something quick and informal -- the size and permanence of the decision justify the added time and expense. A single employee's hallway opinion, a 24-hour online poll, and a ten-customer hallway survey are all far too small and unstructured to support a decision of this scale.

performanceIndicator: Calculate period-over-period percentage change in a metric
question: A boutique's monthly website visits rose from 4,000 in January to 4,600 in February. What is the percentage change in visits?

options.A: A monthly increase of 15% in website visits
options.B: A monthly increase of 13% in website visits
options.C: A monthly increase of 14% in the store's total visits
options.D: A monthly increase of 115% in website visits

explanation: Website visits rose from 4,000 to 4,600, a change of 600, and dividing that change by the starting value of 4,000 gives a 15% increase. The other options divide by the ending value instead (13%), average the two periods before dividing (14%), or report the ratio of new to old without subtracting the base first, which gives 115% rather than the correct 15%.

performanceIndicator: Calculate period-over-period percentage change in a metric
question: A regional gym chain's average monthly membership revenue fell from $180,000 to $162,000 over the quarter. What is the percentage change in average monthly membership revenue?

options.A: A quarterly decrease of 11% in average monthly membership revenue
options.B: A quarterly decrease of 3% in average monthly membership revenue
options.C: A quarterly decrease of 10% in average monthly membership revenue
options.D: A quarterly increase of 10% in average monthly membership revenue

explanation: Membership revenue fell from $180,000 to $162,000, a decline of $18,000, and dividing that decline by the starting value of $180,000 gives a 10% decrease. Dividing by the ending value of $162,000 instead gives 11%, which overstates the decline relative to the correct base period. Treating the quarterly change as if it needed to be spread evenly across the quarter's three months produces the much smaller 3% figure, and simply flipping the direction of the change produces a 10% increase instead of the actual decrease.

performanceIndicator: Compute descriptive statistics (mean, median, percentage) from survey data
question: A coffee shop surveys 150 customers about how many times they visited last week; 30 say they visited exactly twice. What percentage of the 150 respondents visited exactly twice?

options.A: 15% of respondents visited exactly twice
options.B: 25% of respondents visited exactly twice
options.C: 40% of respondents visited exactly twice
options.D: 20% of respondents visited exactly twice

explanation: Thirty of the 150 respondents said they visited exactly twice, and 30 divided by 150 is 20%, the correct share of respondents. The other options divide 30 by the wrong base -- 200 (an original invite count never used here), 120 (an assumed non-response adjustment that doesn't apply), or 75 (half of the actual respondent count) -- each producing a different, incorrect percentage.

performanceIndicator: Compute descriptive statistics (mean, median, percentage) from survey data
question: A survey collects satisfaction ratings on a 1-to-5 scale from 8 customers: 5, 4, 5, 3, 5, 4, 2, 5. What is the median rating?

options.A: 4.5, the group's summary satisfaction rating
options.B: 4.1, the group's summary satisfaction rating
options.C: 3.5, the group's summary satisfaction rating across all eight respondents surveyed
options.D: 5.0, the group's summary satisfaction rating

explanation: Sorting the eight ratings gives 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, and with an even number of values the median is the average of the two middle values, 4 and 5, which is 4.5. Averaging all eight ratings instead gives a mean of 4.1, and averaging only the lowest and highest ratings (2 and 5) gives a range midpoint of 3.5, neither of which is the median. The single most frequent rating, 5, is the mode, a different statistic entirely.

question: PulseWear Fitness wants to know exactly how long customers linger in front of each display before choosing a product, without asking them any questions. Which data-collection method fits best?

options.A: Direct behavioral observation
options.B: A structured mail survey sent after the store visit
options.C: A moderated focus group discussion
options.D: A telephone interview

explanation: Watching and timing customer behavior at the display without asking any questions is direct observation, the method for capturing what people actually do rather than what they say. A mail survey, a focus group, and a phone interview all rely on customers reporting information themselves, which is not what PulseWear wants to measure here.

question: NovaFit Supplements wants a small group of loyal customers to try an unreleased protein bar together in one room, discuss their reactions out loud, and build on each other's comments in real time, with a moderator guiding the conversation. Which data-collection method fits best?

options.A: A private one-on-one phone interview
options.B: A large-scale mail survey sent to the company's entire loyal-customer mailing list
options.C: A focus group, letting participants react to each other's comments
options.D: Passive observation with no discussion at all

explanation: Bringing loyal customers together to react out loud and build on each other's comments, guided by a moderator, is a focus group -- the interactive, moderated format is what distinguishes it from other methods. A one-on-one interview has no group interaction, a mail survey isn't a live discussion at all, and passive observation records behavior without any spoken reaction to build on.

question: Before spending $2 million to launch a new product line, Ferro Appliances commissions a study of customer demand, competitor offerings, and price sensitivity rather than relying on its executives' assumptions. What is the primary reason marketing data matters here?

options.A: It satisfies a routine legal filing requirement
options.B: It reduces the risk of a costly, poorly informed launch decision
options.C: It shifts legal liability for the launch onto the research firm
options.D: It creates a paper trail executives can cite if the decision is later questioned

explanation: Commissioning research on demand, competition, and price sensitivity before a large launch exists to reduce the risk of committing $2 million based on unverified assumptions -- that is the core reason marketing data matters for a decision this size. It is not a legal filing requirement, and while thorough research can create a useful record, that is a side effect, not the primary reason for the study, and no research shifts legal liability onto the firm that conducted it.

question: A firm wants to text-message promotional offers to customers' personal cell phones using an automated system. Which federal law most directly governs this practice?

options.A: The Telephone Consumer Protection Act's texting rules
options.B: A state's general sales tax law
options.C: The federal Truth in Lending Act
options.D: The Children's Online Privacy Act

explanation: Sending automated promotional text messages to personal cell phones is directly governed by the Telephone Consumer Protection Act, which restricts autodialed and prerecorded communications to consumers. State sales tax law, truth-in-lending disclosure rules, and children's online privacy protections each govern a different area entirely and do not apply to this practice.

question: A retailer builds a customer database that links loyalty-card purchase history to individuals' full names, home addresses, and birthdates, then sells that combined file to a third-party data broker without ever asking customers first. Which regulatory concern applies most directly?

options.A: A breach of the retailer's own internal loyalty-program terms
options.B: An antitrust concern over combining competitor data
options.C: A data-privacy consent violation
options.D: A copyright issue over the retailer's original database design and structure

explanation: Selling a file that combines identifiable customer data -- names, addresses, birthdates, and purchase history -- to a third party without consent raises a data-privacy and consent problem, the core regulatory concern with this kind of data sale. It is not primarily a breach of the retailer's own internal program terms, an antitrust issue (no competitor data is involved), or a copyright question over the database's structure, since the concern here is about the personal data itself, not who owns the database design.

question: Sunfield Grocers uses software that automatically combines point-of-sale data, loyalty-app activity, and in-store Wi-Fi location pings into a single daily dashboard for its category managers, without any manual data entry. What marketing-information technology does this describe?

options.A: Automated data integration across multiple in-store sources
options.B: A manual spreadsheet an analyst compiles by copying each source in by hand
options.C: A single point-of-sale terminal
options.D: A customer-facing mobile app used for loyalty rewards

explanation: Software that pulls point-of-sale, loyalty, and location data together automatically into one dashboard, with no manual entry, is automated data integration across the store's separate systems -- combining sources without human copying is the defining feature. The opposite of that is a manually compiled spreadsheet, which is exactly what the automation replaces; a single POS terminal and a standalone loyalty app are just two of the individual sources being combined, not the integration technology itself.

question: A research firm interviews shoppers right outside a store's entrance about their opinions of that same store. What issue does this location raise?

options.A: A poor question-wording problem
options.B: An unusually tiny sample size
options.C: The interviewer's tone influencing shoppers' answers
options.D: Bias toward the store's own current shoppers

explanation: Surveying only people already outside the store's entrance means the sample systematically excludes anyone who does not shop there, which is a selection-bias problem tied to location, not sample size, wording, or interviewer tone. Those three are real research-quality concerns, but none of them explains why interviewing shoppers right at the door specifically skews who gets asked.

question: A nonprofit asks donors face-to-face, 'Do you agree that our organization does important work in the community?' and records their answers on the spot for a satisfaction report. What research issue does this raise?

options.A: A sampling frame error, since only current donors were asked
options.B: A coding error introduced when responses are later entered
options.C: Social-desirability bias, since face-to-face donors may feel pressure to agree
options.D: A nonresponse error among the donor population

explanation: Asking a leading, agreement-framed question face to face invites social-desirability bias, since donors may feel pressure to give the positive answer the asker seems to want rather than their honest opinion. This is not a sampling frame problem (the right population, donors, was asked), a data-entry coding error (nothing was mis-entered), or a nonresponse error (everyone asked did respond) -- the distortion comes from how and by whom the question was asked.

question: A quality inspector selects every 20th item coming off a production line for a defect check, starting from a randomly chosen first item. What type of sample is this?

options.A: A judgment sample based on the inspector's opinion
options.B: A systematic sample using a fixed interval
options.C: A census of all items
options.D: A quota sample by shift

explanation: Selecting every 20th item after a random start is a systematic sample, which uses a fixed interval applied to the whole line rather than pure judgment, a full census, or fixed quotas by shift. A judgment sample would rely on the inspector's subjective opinion about which items look risky, a census would check every single item, and a quota sample would set fixed numbers per shift rather than sampling at a fixed interval.

question: A research firm hired by a snack brand designs its survey questions so that nearly any honest answer a respondent gives can be summarized in the final report as support for launching the brand's new product. What ethical issue does this raise?

options.A: Research design built toward a predetermined conclusion
options.B: Failure to pay respondents a fair incentive
options.C: Using a sample too small to represent the target market
options.D: Sharing the raw survey data with a second, unrelated client without additional permission

explanation: Designing questions so that almost any honest answer gets summarized as support for the client's desired outcome is biased research design aimed at a predetermined conclusion, which misrepresents what the research actually found. It is not primarily about incentive pay, sample size, or sharing data with another client -- the ethical problem here is that the research process itself was rigged to reach a foregone conclusion regardless of what respondents actually said.

question: A cereal brand runs a six-week study measuring how a new box design affects shelf sales before rolling it out nationwide. What best describes this activity?

options.A: Basic research meant to advance general marketing theory
options.B: A routine internal sales audit
options.C: A financial statement review
options.D: Applied marketing research for one decision

explanation: Running a time-limited study to inform one specific decision -- whether to roll out a new box design -- is applied marketing research, aimed at solving a particular business problem. It is not basic research (which builds general theory rather than answering one company's question), a sales audit, or a financial statement review.

question: Rather than test one specific product decision, a beverage company funds a multi-year university study exploring how brand loyalty forms in adolescents generally, with no immediate commercial application planned. What best describes this activity?

options.A: Basic research building general knowledge with no immediate decision to inform
options.B: Applied research aimed squarely at one upcoming packaging decision the company must make
options.C: A routine internal competitive-pricing audit each quarter
options.D: A one-time internal customer satisfaction survey

explanation: Funding open-ended, long-term research into how brand loyalty forms generally, with no specific decision attached, is basic research -- it builds general understanding rather than answering one applied business question. Applied research is the opposite: aimed squarely at a specific upcoming decision, which is not what is described here, and neither a routine pricing audit nor a one-time satisfaction survey involves the multi-year, theory-building scope this study has.

question: Vantage Hardware sets up an ongoing process that continuously gathers sales figures, customer feedback, and competitor pricing, then gets each piece to the right manager when they need it. What is this process called?

options.A: A single one-time market survey
options.B: A marketing information system routing data as needed
options.C: A routine accounting reconciliation process
options.D: An unrelated payroll database system

explanation: An ongoing system that continuously gathers sales, feedback, and competitor data and routes it to the managers who need it is a marketing information system -- the continuous, routed nature is what distinguishes it from a one-time survey. It is also not an accounting reconciliation process or a payroll database, which handle entirely different kinds of information.

question: A retailer has ten years of raw, unsorted sales transactions. Before analysts can spot any useful pattern, what must first be done to the data?

options.A: Encrypt it for storage
options.B: Convert it into a standardized accounting ledger format
options.C: Clean, organize, and summarize it
options.D: Sell it to a data broker

explanation: Raw, unsorted transactions have to be cleaned, organized, and summarized before analysts can spot any useful pattern -- that processing step turns raw data into something usable. Converting it into an accounting ledger, encrypting it, or selling it to a broker are all different actions that do not prepare the data for analysis.

question: An analytics team receives millions of individual customer transactions from the past year and needs to identify the ten product categories driving the most repeat purchases, so they can be highlighted in an executive summary. What data-processing step accomplishes this?

options.A: Manually re-keying every individual transaction into a spreadsheet one row at a time
options.B: Encrypting the transaction file before it is shared
options.C: Aggregating transactions by category and ranking them by repeat-purchase volume
options.D: Deleting duplicate customer transaction records first

explanation: To surface the ten categories driving the most repeat purchases out of millions of transactions, the team needs to aggregate transactions by category and rank them by repeat-purchase volume -- summarizing at the category level is what makes a pattern visible. Manually re-keying every transaction by hand does not summarize anything, encrypting the file is a security step unrelated to analysis, and removing duplicate records alone would not identify which categories drive repeat purchases.

performanceIndicator: Identify data monitored for marketing decisions
question: Fernbrook Outfitters wants to know which of its email subject lines gets more people to actually open the message. Which piece of data should it monitor?

options.A: Total number of items sold
options.B: Average time customers spend browsing the website
options.C: Warehouse inventory turnover
options.D: Email open rate

explanation: To find out which subject line gets more people to open an email, the relevant data is the email open rate itself -- the metric that directly measures that behavior. Items sold, browsing time, and warehouse turnover all measure something else entirely and would not show which subject line performs better at getting the email opened.

question: A survey asks, 'Don't you agree that our checkout process is fast and easy?' and records whether each shopper says yes or no. What research error does this illustrate?

options.A: A late mailing error
options.B: A data-entry error made when typing responses in later
options.C: A leading question that pushes toward yes
options.D: An undercoverage sampling error

explanation: Phrasing a question as 'Don't you agree...' is a leading question -- it pushes respondents toward a particular answer rather than measuring their true opinion. This is not a late mailing, a data-entry mistake made afterward, or a sampling coverage gap; the flaw is baked into the question's wording itself.

question: A researcher conducting phone interviews reads each question in a flat, hurried tone for the negative options and a warm, enthusiastic tone for the positive options, without realizing it. What research error does this illustrate?

options.A: A sampling frame error, since the wrong population received the calls
options.B: Interviewer bias introduced unintentionally through vocal tone
options.C: A coding error introduced later when answers are entered into the analysis software
options.D: A low overall response rate

explanation: Unconsciously reading positive options warmly and negative options flatly is interviewer bias -- the interviewer's own delivery, not the respondent's true opinion, is shaping the answers. This is not a sampling frame problem (the right people were called), a later coding error (the distortion happens during the interview itself, before any data entry), or simply a low response rate, since the people who did respond are the ones being influenced.

question: After a popular podcast host mentions Cinderfield Coffee unprompted during an episode, the company wants to know how people are reacting online. What should it monitor?

options.A: In-store foot traffic counts
options.B: Weekly payroll expense totals
options.C: Social-media mentions and sentiment about the brand
options.D: Shipping delivery time averages

explanation: After unprompted buzz like a podcast mention, the useful thing to track is social-media mentions and sentiment about the brand, since that shows how the public is actually reacting. Foot traffic, payroll expenses, and shipping times are all real business metrics, but none of them measures the online reaction the company is asking about here.

question: A wholesaler lists an order at $5,000 and offers a trade discount series of 20/10/5. What is the net price after all three discounts?

options.A: $3,250, the price after the discount series
options.B: $3,420, the price after the discount series
options.C: $4,000, the price after the discount series
options.D: $3,600, the price after the discount series

explanation: Applying the discounts in sequence, $5,000 x 0.80 x 0.90 x 0.95 gives a net price of $3,420. The other options either add the discount percentages together for a flat 35% off ($3,250), apply only the first discount ($4,000), or stop after the first two discounts and skip the last 5% ($3,600).

question: Meridian Distributors lists a shipment at $12,000 and offers a trade discount series of 25/15/10. What amount does Meridian ultimately collect after the discount series is applied?

options.A: $6,000, the resulting net invoice price
options.B: $6,885, the resulting net invoice price
options.C: $9,000, the resulting net invoice price
options.D: $7,650, the resulting net invoice price

explanation: Chaining the discounts in sequence, $12,000 x 0.75 x 0.85 x 0.90 gives a net invoice price of $6,885. Adding the three percentages together for a flat 50% off instead gives $6,000, which understates the true chained result. Stopping after only the first discount gives $9,000, and stopping after the first two discounts, before applying the final 10%, gives $7,650 -- neither reflects the full three-step series.

performanceIndicator: Calculate break-even point in units and dollars
question: A product sells for $25 per unit, has a variable cost of $15 per unit, and the business carries $8,000 in total fixed costs. How many units must it sell to break even?

options.A: 800 units to break even
options.B: 320 units to break even
options.C: 533 units to break even
options.D: 200 units to break even for the new product line

explanation: Break-even units equal fixed costs divided by the contribution margin per unit ($25 minus $15 equals $10), so $8,000 divided by $10 is 800 units. The other options divide the fixed costs by the selling price alone (320), by the variable cost alone (533), or by the sum of price and variable cost (200), none of which is the contribution margin.

question: A retailer buys 50 units at $27 each, originally prices them at $50 retail, then marks the entire lot down to $42 to clear it out and sells all 50 units at that price. What is the maintained markup percentage, based on the price actually charged?

options.A: 46.0% maintained markup
options.B: 55.6% maintained markup
options.C: 35.7% maintained markup
options.D: 16.0% maintained markup

explanation: Maintained markup is figured on the price actually charged, so ($42 minus $27) divided by $42 gives 35.7%. The other options compute markup against the original $50 retail price instead of the actual selling price (46.0%), compute markup on cost rather than on the selling price (55.6%), or report the markdown percentage off the original retail price (16.0%), which is a different measure entirely.

question: A boutique buys 40 jackets at $45 each, originally prices them at $75, marks the entire lot down to $60, and sells all 40 jackets at that price. What is the maintained markup percentage, based on the price actually charged?

options.A: A maintained markup of 25.0% on the actual selling price
options.B: A maintained markup of 33.3% on the actual selling price
options.C: A maintained markup of 40.0% on the actual selling price
options.D: A maintained markup of 20.0% on the actual selling price

explanation: Maintained markup is figured on the price actually charged, so ($60 minus $45) divided by $60 gives 25.0%. Computing the markup against the original $75 retail price instead of the actual $60 selling price gives 40.0%, and computing markup on the $45 cost rather than on the selling price gives 33.3%. The 20.0% figure is the markdown percentage off the original retail price -- a different measure from maintained markup entirely.

question: A coat originally priced at $120 is marked down to $90, then marked down again to $72. What is the total markdown percentage from the original price?

options.A: 45.0% total markdown
options.B: 40.0% total markdown
options.C: 66.7% total markdown from the original coat price
options.D: 20.0% total markdown

explanation: The coat fell from $120 to $72, a total markdown of $48, and $48 divided by the original $120 price is 40.0%. The other options add the two sequential markdown percentages together instead of computing the total directly (45.0%), divide the total markdown by the final price instead of the original (66.7%), or count only the second markdown and ignore the first (20.0%).

question: An item costs a retailer $60 and is priced to sell at $84. What is the markup percentage based on cost?

options.A: 28.6% markup on the item's cost
options.B: 71.4% markup on the item's cost
options.C: 140.0% markup on the item's cost
options.D: 40.0% markup on the item's cost

explanation: Markup on cost is the dollar markup divided by the cost, so ($84 minus $60) divided by $60 gives 40.0%. The other options compute the markup against the $84 selling price instead of cost (28.6%), express the cost as a percentage of the retail price instead of computing markup (71.4%), or report the full retail-to-cost ratio without subtracting 1 first (140.0%).

question: A retailer buys an item for $50 and prices it to sell at $80. What is the markup percentage based on retail (margin)?

options.A: 37.5% markup on retail
options.B: 60.0% markup on retail
options.C: 62.5% markup on retail
options.D: 160.0% markup on retail

explanation: Markup on retail (margin) is the dollar markup divided by the selling price, so ($80 minus $50) divided by $80 gives 37.5%. The other options compute the markup against the $50 cost instead of the retail price (60.0%), express the cost as a percentage of the retail price rather than computing a markup at all (62.5%), or report the retail-to-cost ratio without subtracting 1 first (160.0%).

performanceIndicator: Convert markup on cost to markup on retail
question: A retailer applies a 25% markup on cost to an item. What is the equivalent markup percentage on retail (selling price)?

options.A: 25.0% markup on retail for the same item
options.B: 20.0% markup on retail
options.C: 12.5% markup on retail
options.D: 33.3% markup on retail

explanation: Converting markup on cost to markup on retail uses the formula (markup on cost) / (1 + markup on cost), so 0.25 / 1.25 gives 20.0%. The other options simply restate the 25% cost-based figure as if it applied to retail unchanged (25.0%), guess at roughly half the cost markup (12.5%), or divide by (1 minus the markup) instead of (1 plus the markup), producing 33.3%.

performanceIndicator: Convert markup on cost to markup on retail
question: A furniture store applies a 75% markup on cost to a sofa. What is the equivalent markup percentage on retail (selling price)?

options.A: A markup of 37.5% on the sofa's retail price
options.B: A markup of 75.0% on the retail price of the newly imported sofa
options.C: A markup of 300.0% on the sofa's retail price
options.D: A markup of 42.9% on the sofa's retail price

explanation: Converting markup on cost to markup on retail uses the formula (markup on cost) divided by (1 + markup on cost), so 0.75 divided by 1.75 gives 42.9%. Restating the 75% cost-based markup as if it applied directly to retail gives 75.0%, guessing at roughly half the cost markup gives 37.5%, and dividing by (1 minus the markup) instead of (1 plus the markup) gives 300.0% -- all three miss the correct conversion formula.

question: An electronics retailer marks every television with a red 'Was $999, Now $699!' tag, but the televisions were never actually sold at $999 -- that price existed only on the tag itself. What pricing ethics issue does this illustrate?

options.A: Aggressive predatory pricing tactics
options.B: Illegal price-fixing with competitors
options.C: A deceptive reference price that was never real
options.D: Unlawful regional price discrimination

explanation: Advertising a 'was' price that the item was never actually sold at is a deceptive reference-price claim, since it fabricates a comparison to make the current price look like a bargain. It is not predatory pricing (pricing below cost to eliminate a rival), illegal price-fixing (which requires an agreement with competitors), or price discrimination (charging different customers different prices), none of which describes a fake reference price.

performanceIndicator: Determine cash discount and net amount (terms of sale)
question: A retailer receives a $6,000 invoice with terms of 2/10, net 30, and pays within the 10-day discount period. What is the net amount due?

options.A: $5,880 net amount due
options.B: $6,000 net amount due
options.C: $5,400 net amount due on the invoice payment
options.D: $5,760 net amount due

explanation: Paying within the discount window earns the 2% cash discount, so $6,000 minus 2% of $6,000 ($120) leaves $5,880 due. The other options assume the discount was missed entirely ($6,000), mistake the '10' in the terms for a 10% discount rate ($5,400), or apply the 2% discount twice ($5,760).

performanceIndicator: Determine cash discount and net amount (terms of sale)
question: A distributor receives a $15,000 invoice with terms of 3/15, net 45, and pays on day 10, within the discount period. What is the net amount due?

options.A: A net amount of $12,750 due on the distributor's invoice
options.B: A net amount of $15,000 due on the invoice
options.C: A net amount of $14,550 due on the distributor's invoice for the equipment order
options.D: A net amount of $14,100 due on the invoice payment

explanation: Paying within the discount period earns the 3% cash discount, so $15,000 minus 3% of $15,000 ($450) leaves $14,550 due. Assuming the discount was missed entirely leaves the full $15,000, mistaking the '15' in the terms for a 15% discount rate gives $12,750, and applying the 3% discount twice gives $14,100 -- none of which reflects the actual 3/15 terms correctly applied once.

question: A buyer's invoice cost is $36 per unit. What is the keystone retail price?

options.A: $72.00 keystone price
options.B: $54.00 keystone price
options.C: $18.00 keystone price
options.D: $108.00 keystone price for the retailer's unit

explanation: Keystone pricing simply doubles the invoice cost, so $36 x 2 gives a keystone retail price of $72.00. The other options mistakenly halve the cost instead of doubling it ($18.00), add only a 50% markup instead of a full keystone markup ($54.00), or triple the cost instead of doubling it ($108.00).

question: A buyer's invoice cost is $58 per unit, and the retailer wants a keystone-plus price, adding an extra 10% of cost on top of the standard keystone markup. What is the resulting retail price?

options.A: A retail price of $116.00 for the unit
options.B: A retail price of $127.60 for the unit
options.C: A retail price of $63.80 for the retailer's newly stocked seasonal unit
options.D: A retail price of $121.80 for the unit

explanation: Standard keystone doubles the $58 cost to $116.00, and the extra 10% of cost adds $5.80 (10% of $58), for a keystone-plus price of $121.80. Stopping at the plain keystone price without the extra addition gives $116.00, computing the extra 10% on the $116.00 keystone price instead of on the original cost gives $127.60, and adding 10% of cost without doubling for keystone at all gives only $63.80.

performanceIndicator: Determine selling price to achieve a target margin
question: An item costs a retailer $56, and the retailer wants a 30% margin, based on the selling price. What selling price should it set?

options.A: $72.80 selling price for the item
options.B: $43.08 selling price for the item
options.C: $80.00 selling price for the item
options.D: $86.00 selling price for the item

explanation: To hit a margin based on selling price, cost is divided by (1 minus the margin), so $56 divided by 0.70 gives $80.00. The other options add 30% of cost as if it were a cost-based markup instead of a price-based margin ($72.80), divide by (1 plus the margin) instead of (1 minus the margin) ($43.08), or add a flat $30 instead of applying the percentage correctly ($86.00).

performanceIndicator: Determine selling price to achieve a target margin
question: An item costs a distributor $114, and it wants a 25% margin based on the selling price, plus a flat $6 handling fee added to the price after the margin is set. What selling price should it charge the retailer?

options.A: A selling price of $152.00 for the distributor's newly received bulk item shipment
options.B: A selling price of $158.00 for the item
options.C: A selling price of $148.50 for the distributor's item
options.D: A selling price of $160.00 for the distributor's item

explanation: To reach a 25% margin based on selling price, $114 is divided by 0.75, giving $152.00, and then the flat $6 handling fee is added on top for a final price of $158.00. Leaving out the handling fee entirely gives just $152.00; treating the 25% as a markup on cost instead of a margin on price, then adding the fee, gives $148.50; and adding the $6 fee to the cost before dividing by 0.75 gives $160.00 instead of adding it after.

question: GreenCart Grocery installs electronic shelf labels that automatically raise the price of bottled water and batteries a few hours before a forecasted severe storm, based on real-time weather-data feeds, without any employee changing a single tag by hand. What pricing technology does this describe?

options.A: A weekly manual price-review meeting
options.B: A printed paper price list updated by hand once each month by store staff
options.C: A fixed, storewide seasonal discount calendar set each year
options.D: Automated dynamic pricing driven by real-time external data feeds

explanation: Electronic shelf labels that adjust prices automatically based on live weather data, with no manual tag changes, describe automated dynamic pricing driven by real-time external data feeds -- the automation and the external data trigger are the defining features. A manual weekly review, a printed list updated monthly by hand, and a fixed seasonal discount calendar are all much slower, manual approaches that could not react to a storm forecast hours in advance.

question: A vendor offers a co-op advertising allowance equal to 5% of a retailer's purchases. The retailer buys $60,000 of the vendor's product during the period and submits proof of a qualifying ad campaign. What reimbursement is the retailer owed?

options.A: $1,500 co-op reimbursement
options.B: $3,000 co-op reimbursement
options.C: $6,000 co-op reimbursement for the ad campaign
options.D: $60,000 co-op reimbursement

explanation: The co-op allowance is 5% of $60,000 in qualifying purchases, which is $3,000. The other options apply half the stated rate ($1,500), apply double the stated rate ($6,000), or treat the full $60,000 purchase amount as the reimbursement itself ($60,000).

question: A vendor's co-op program reimburses 50% of a retailer's approved ad spend, up to a cap of 3% of the retailer's purchases from the vendor. The retailer spends $2,000 on a qualifying ad campaign and purchased $50,000 of the vendor's product this period. What reimbursement does the retailer receive?

options.A: A reimbursement of $1,000 to the retailer
options.B: A reimbursement of $1,500 to the retailer for its qualifying ad campaign
options.C: A reimbursement of $2,000 to the retailer for the campaign
options.D: A reimbursement of $60 to the retailer

explanation: Fifty percent of the $2,000 ad spend is $1,000, and the 3% cap on $50,000 in purchases is $1,500, so the retailer receives the smaller of the two: $1,000. Reimbursing the full $1,500 cap regardless of actual spend ignores that the cap is a ceiling, not a guaranteed amount; reimbursing the full $2,000 ad spend ignores the 50% share entirely; and applying the 3% cap to the ad spend instead of to purchases gives only $60.

performanceIndicator: Calculate cost per rating point (CPP) and GRPs
question: A radio ad schedule runs 6 airings that together deliver a total of 30 rating points, at a total cost of $9,000. What is the cost per rating point (CPP)?

options.A: $1,500.00 per rating point
options.B: $600.00 per rating point for the radio schedule
options.C: $300.00 per rating point
options.D: $225.00 per rating point

explanation: CPP is total cost divided by total rating points, so $9,000 divided by 30 rating points gives $300.00. The other options divide the cost by the number of airings instead of rating points ($1,500.00), by half the actual rating points ($600.00), or by an inflated rating-point total ($225.00).

performanceIndicator: Calculate cost per thousand (CPM) for advertising media
question: A digital ad buy costs $2,400 and delivers 800,000 impressions. What is the cost per thousand impressions (CPM)?

options.A: $3.00 per thousand impressions
options.B: $30.00 per thousand impressions
options.C: $0.33 per thousand impressions on the digital ad buy
options.D: $0.30 per thousand impressions

explanation: CPM is the total cost divided by the number of thousands of impressions delivered, so $2,400 divided by 800 (800,000 impressions divided by 1,000) gives $3.00. The other options divide by ten times too many thousands ($30.00), invert the ratio of impressions to cost ($0.33), or divide by hundreds instead of thousands ($0.30).

performanceIndicator: Calculate coupon redemption cost and rate
question: A brand distributes 250,000 coupons with a $0.50 face value. The redemption rate is 4%, and the retailer charges a $0.08 handling fee per redeemed coupon. What is the total redemption cost?

options.A: $145,000 total redemption cost for the campaign
options.B: $5,800 total redemption cost
options.C: $5,000 total redemption cost
options.D: $6,600 total redemption cost

explanation: Only the redeemed coupons count: 4% of 250,000 is 10,000 coupons, and each one costs $0.50 face value plus the $0.08 handling fee, or $0.58, for a total of $5,800. The other options apply the cost to every distributed coupon instead of just the redeemed ones ($145,000), leave out the handling fee entirely ($5,000), or double-count the handling fee ($6,600).

performanceIndicator: Calculate coupon redemption cost and rate
question: A grocery chain distributes 600,000 coupons with a $1.25 face value and pays retailers a $0.10 handling fee per redeemed coupon. Historically this brand's coupons redeem at 3%. What is the total expected redemption cost?

options.A: A total expected redemption cost of $24,300 for the grocery chain's campaign
options.B: A total expected redemption cost of $22,500 for the coupons
options.C: A total expected redemption cost of $810,000
options.D: A total expected redemption cost of $26,100

explanation: Only the redeemed coupons count: 3% of 600,000 is 18,000 coupons, and each one costs $1.25 face value plus the $0.10 handling fee, or $1.35, for a total expected cost of $24,300. Leaving out the handling fee gives $22,500 instead, applying the cost to all 600,000 distributed coupons rather than just the 3% that redeem gives $810,000, and doubling the handling fee gives $26,100.

performanceIndicator: Calculate reach, frequency, and gross impressions
question: A campaign reaches 60% of a 300,000-person target market with an average frequency of 4 exposures per person. What are the gross impressions delivered?

options.A: 180,000 gross impressions
options.B: 720,000 gross impressions
options.C: 1,200,000 gross impressions across the target market
options.D: 72,000,000 gross impressions

explanation: Gross impressions equal the number of people reached times the average frequency, so 60% of 300,000 (180,000 people) times 4 exposures gives 720,000 gross impressions. The other options report just the number of people reached without multiplying by frequency (180,000), apply the frequency to the entire target market instead of just the people reached (1,200,000), or fail to convert the 60% reach to a decimal before multiplying (72,000,000).

performanceIndicator: Calculate reach, frequency, and gross impressions
question: A streaming ad campaign reaches 45% of a 900,000-person audience with an average frequency of 6 exposures. What are the gross impressions delivered?

options.A: 5,400,000 gross impressions delivered by the campaign
options.B: 2,430,000 gross impressions delivered by the campaign
options.C: 405,000 gross impressions delivered by the campaign
options.D: 243,000,000 gross impressions delivered by the campaign

explanation: Gross impressions equal the number of people reached times the average frequency, so 45% of 900,000 (405,000 people) times 6 exposures gives 2,430,000 gross impressions. Applying the frequency to the entire 900,000-person audience instead of just the people actually reached gives 5,400,000, reporting the number reached without multiplying by frequency at all gives only 405,000, and failing to convert the 45% reach to a decimal before multiplying gives an inflated 243,000,000.

question: A skincare brand pays a well-known dermatologist to appear in an ad reciting a script the brand wrote, presenting claims as the dermatologist's own independent clinical opinion, even though she has no personal experience with how the product performs. What ethical issue does this illustrate?

options.A: A simple failure to disclose the sponsorship itself
options.B: An unrelated copyright licensing dispute over the music
options.C: A false expert-endorsement claim, since the dermatologist never tested the product
options.D: An unrelated FTC pricing-disclosure violation

explanation: Presenting a paid script as the dermatologist's own independent clinical opinion, when the dermatologist never actually tested the product, is a false expert-endorsement claim -- the endorsement itself misrepresents genuine expert use and testing, not merely who paid for the ad. This is a different problem from simply failing to disclose the sponsorship (the ad could disclose payment and still falsely claim clinical testing), and it has nothing to do with copyright licensing or a separate pricing-disclosure issue.

question: An online retailer sends bulk marketing emails to customers but provides no way for recipients to opt out of future messages. Which federal law does this violate?

options.A: State sales tax law
options.B: The Truth in Lending Act
options.C: The CAN-SPAM Act's opt-out requirement
options.D: The Children's Online Privacy Act's consent rule

explanation: Sending bulk marketing emails with no opt-out option violates the CAN-SPAM Act, which requires commercial email to include a working opt-out mechanism. State sales tax law, truth-in-lending disclosure rules, and children's online privacy protections each govern a completely different area and do not apply to this practice.

question: Meadowlane Furniture uses software that automatically shows each website visitor a different homepage banner based on that visitor's past browsing and purchase history, without any employee choosing which banner to display. What promotion technology does this describe?

options.A: Automated personalization driven by visitor browsing data
options.B: A single fixed banner shown to every website visitor equally
options.C: A manually rotated set of banners an employee swaps weekly
options.D: A print catalog mailed to every customer regardless of browsing history

explanation: Software that automatically tailors each visitor's banner based on their own browsing and purchase history, with no employee choosing it, is automated personalization driven by visitor data -- the automatic, individualized targeting is the defining feature. A single fixed banner shown to everyone, a set an employee manually rotates, and a print catalog mailed to the whole list are all the same message for every recipient, which is the opposite of what personalization technology does.

question: A first-time customer at Hollow Creek Bakery posts an unprompted photo of her order on social media, tagging the bakery, with no discount or incentive offered by the bakery in exchange. What promotion channel does this represent?

options.A: A paid influencer sponsorship deal
options.B: A loyalty-program point redemption
options.C: A printed newspaper coupon offer
options.D: Organic word-of-mouth, with nothing offered in return

explanation: A customer posting unprompted, with no discount or incentive from the bakery, is organic word-of-mouth -- genuine, unpaid advocacy is what defines the channel. A paid influencer deal, a loyalty-point redemption, and a printed coupon offer are all forms of promotion the business initiates and controls, which is the opposite of this customer-driven post.

question: Members of an online forum dedicated to home espresso equipment spontaneously start a long discussion thread comparing a new machine's features, with no brand employee ever participating in or seeding the conversation. What promotion channel does this represent?

options.A: A brand-sponsored influencer unboxing video campaign
options.B: A paid search advertisement placement
options.C: A company-seeded discussion thread the brand secretly started and monitored throughout
options.D: Organic online word-of-mouth among the forum's own members

explanation: A spontaneous discussion among forum members themselves, with no brand employee seeding or joining it, is organic online word-of-mouth -- the conversation belongs entirely to the community, not the brand. A sponsored unboxing video, a paid search ad, and a company-seeded thread the brand secretly started are all brand-initiated promotion, which is the opposite of genuine, unprompted peer discussion.

question: A firm's sales were $300,000 last year and are forecast to grow 10% this year. The firm sets its total promotional budget at 5% of forecast sales. What is the promotional budget?

options.A: $30,000 promotional budget
options.B: $15,000 promotional budget
options.C: $33,000 promotional budget
options.D: $16,500 promotional budget

explanation: Forecast sales are $300,000 grown by 10%, or $330,000, and 5% of that forecast is $16,500. The other options apply the 5% to last year's sales instead of the forecast ($15,000), use the 10% growth rate itself as the budget percentage ($33,000), or set the budget equal to the dollar growth in sales rather than a percentage of forecast sales ($30,000).

question: A retailer's sales were $850,000 last year and are forecast to grow 8% this year. The retailer allocates 6% of forecast sales to promotion, split evenly across three channels. What is the promotional budget for each individual channel?

options.A: A channel budget of $17,000 for each promotional channel
options.B: A channel budget of $24,480 for each promotional channel
options.C: A promotional budget of $55,080 for the retailer's marketing plan this year
options.D: A channel budget of $18,360 for each promotional channel

explanation: Forecast sales are $850,000 grown by 8%, or $918,000; 6% of that is $55,080 total, and split evenly across three channels that is $18,360 each. Applying the 6% to last year's $850,000 instead of the forecast, then splitting three ways, gives $17,000 per channel; using the 8% growth rate itself as the budget percentage, split three ways, gives $24,480 per channel; and reporting the $55,080 total without dividing it across the three channels overstates any single channel's share.

question: After a product recall makes national news, a manufacturer's PR team schedules a series of calls specifically with the reporters and editors who cover its industry, ahead of any other communication, to make sure the company's account of events runs before rumors spread. Which PR audience is the team prioritizing?

options.A: The company's own internal employees, informed after the media
options.B: The news media that covers this industry
options.C: Government regulators overseeing the recall process
options.D: The general public, reached through the company's own social-media channels

explanation: Scheduling calls with the reporters and editors who cover the industry, ahead of any other outreach, prioritizes the news media -- the audience with the power to shape how the story first reaches everyone else. This is not primarily aimed at internal employees, government regulators, or the general public reached through social media, since those calls are made specifically to journalists before any broader communication goes out.

question: A radio ad for a mattress store ends with, 'Sale ends Sunday -- visit MattressHaven.com or call 555-0199 today.' What advertisement component is this?

options.A: The headline meant to grab the listener's attention
options.B: The ad's call to action
options.C: The brand's tagline
options.D: The body copy explaining product features

explanation: Telling the listener exactly what to do right now -- visit the website or call the number before the sale ends -- is the call to action, the component that prompts an immediate response. It is not the headline (which grabs attention up front), the tagline (a short, memorable brand phrase), or body copy (the explanatory detail about the product), none of which is a direct instruction to act.

question: A cookware brand calls a list of past customers directly on the phone to walk each one individually through a new product's features and take orders on the spot, with no retail store or website involved in that particular sale. What direct marketing channel does this represent?

options.A: A retail in-store demonstration led by a sales associate on the showroom floor
options.B: A billboard advertisement along the highway
options.C: Telemarketing, since the brand contacts customers directly by phone
options.D: A direct-response television commercial with an on-screen order number

explanation: Calling past customers directly and taking orders over the phone, with no store or website in that transaction, is telemarketing -- direct, one-to-one phone contact is what defines the channel.
